c1.story:
Here is a strange way to run a business: get paid not for what you deliver, but for being ready to deliver it. That is how India pays the owners of its big transmission lines. Power Grid does not earn more when more electricity flows through its towers. It earns a regulator-set return on the cost of the line, as long as the line is available, switched on and ready, almost all the time. A heatwave that doubles the load on a line does not double the revenue. A tower knocked down in a cyclone, on the other hand, costs money.

That makes the first door of this industry, the regulated wire owners, feel less like a power company and more like a bond. Power Grid, Adani Energy Solutions and the Powergrid InvIT, a listed trust that owns finished lines and pays out most of its cash, earn a fixed return for decades. Their growth comes from one place only: building more wire. Their value moves with one thing above all: the price of money.

A wire owner is an interest-rate stock dressed as a utility.

The second door makes the stuff the wires are made of. Conductor makers like Diamond Power string aluminium and steel into the bare cable hung between towers; Genus Power makes the smart meters that discoms are installing across the country. They win tenders, buy metal and deliver months later. Their profit lives in the gap between the metal price on the day they quoted and the day they bought.

The third door is the thinnest. Traders like PTC buy power from one utility and sell it to another for a sliver per unit. Contractors like Reliance Infrastructure build someone else's line or substation at a fixed contract price, hoping steel and aluminium do not jump halfway through, and then wait for a state utility to pay them.

Same industry, three temperaments: the bond, the capex-cycle stock and the working-capital stock. The same headline moves each differently.
c1.read:
Three tiles, three doors. Read each top to bottom.

  • The name and the line under it tell you how each earns: a regulated return on assets as long as they stay available; a price per tonne or per meter against tenders; a thin margin per unit traded or a fixed contract price.
  • The tickers are listed companies behind each door. Click any to open its stock page. PGINVIT is the trust that owns lines spun out of Power Grid, so it behaves like Power Grid with the growth removed and the dividend turned up.
  • The bar shows how much of the profit the company keeps. This industry gives you a clean staircase: wire owners at high, cable and meter makers at medium, traders and contractors at low. Unlike in some industries, here the safest business also keeps the most, because the regulator guarantees its slice.
  • The last line is the bet: on how much grid gets built and how cheaply it is financed; on the order book and tame metal prices; on execution and timely payment.

The analogy below the tiles maps directly: the toll-road owner paid whether or not cars come, the shop selling tar and crash barriers to road builders, and the contractor laying the road at a fixed price. Then read the so-what, which is the key to every other card on this page: a wire owner is an interest-rate stock, a cable maker a capex-cycle stock, a contractor a working-capital stock. When you see a rate cut, a metals rally or a discom payment delay in the news, you already know which tile it is talking to.

c2.story:
Follow a unit of electricity from a solar park at Bhadla in the Rajasthan desert to a ceiling fan in Patna. It leaves the park through a pooling substation, gets stepped up to very high voltage, and travels hundreds of kilometres along steel towers strung with aluminium conductor. Somewhere along the way it may ride an HVDC link, high-voltage direct current, the technology for moving huge amounts of power over long distances with fewer losses. Near its destination it is stepped down again, handed to a state network, stepped down once more, and finally metered into a home.

Every stage of that journey had to be built by someone. The kitchen starts with metal. Hindalco, Vedanta and Nalco supply the aluminium for conductors; copper goes into cables and transformer windings. The special silicon steel inside every transformer core, called CRGO, is largely imported from Japan, Korea and China.

Next, equipment. Conductor, cable and meter makers, including Diamond Power and Genus from our list, sit alongside multinationals like Hitachi Energy, Siemens and GE Vernova, which make the heavy transformers and switchgear. Then construction: EPC contractors such as KEC, Kalpataru and L&T, plus Reliance Infrastructure and BF Utilities from the list, erect towers and string lines. Then ownership: Power Grid, Adani Energy Solutions and the InvIT own the finished lines, and Grid-India despatches the power. Finally, state discoms deliver it to the customer.

Notice where the Indian listed names cluster: across three middle stations, from equipment to construction to ownership. Notice where China is. After the border clash at Galwan in 2020, India required clearance for power equipment from neighbouring countries that share a land border, which effectively shut China out of the grid. That protects Indian makers. It also lengthens the queue for transformers, because China was a big part of the world's spare capacity.
c2.read:
Read the five boxes left to right, from raw metal to the meter on your wall, then the two band rows below.

The boxes are metals and steel, equipment makers, EPC and construction, transmission owners, and distribution with the customer. Under each, what happens and who stands there. Watch the names change: metal producers and steel importers at the start; Diamond, Genus and the multinationals at equipment; KEC, Kalpataru, L&T and Reliance Infrastructure at construction; Power Grid, Adani Energy Solutions and the InvIT as owners; state discoms at the end.

The first band row shows who holds each station. The India listed colour covers three stations in a row, two to four, with the equipment band shared with multinationals. That is a wider Indian footprint than in most industries on this page: listed India builds, makes and owns the grid. The first and last bands, metal makers and state discoms, belong to others.

The second band row shows where the rival, China, stands, repeated across the first four stations, with World at the end. Read it as a reminder of what policy has done: China would naturally compete at every one of those stations, especially metals and equipment, and since 2020 it is kept out of the grid by import curbs. The rival row shows the threat that a policy change would let back in.

The so-what under the diagram gives the risk map: owners sit at the safest station, equipment makers carry metal and capacity risk, and the whole chain depends on the last box, discoms, paying on time. The note adds geography: the grid is being built where the renewables are, in Rajasthan, Gujarat, Karnataka and the Ladakh corridor.

c3.story:
If you want to forecast demand for a cable maker or a tower contractor, you will learn more from the Union budget speech than from any consumer survey. Most demand in this industry is government demand, decided by planners in Delhi and state capitals.

The biggest buyer is the central transmission planner, through Power Grid and through lines auctioned to private bidders. India has set out a roadmap to connect half a terawatt of renewable capacity by 2030, and every solar and wind park on that path needs an evacuation line and a pooling substation. So renewable auction results are, in effect, transmission orders with a delay. A park awarded today needs its line ordered within about a year.

State transmission utilities buy intra-state lines and substations, paid for out of state budgets and central schemes, and they spend more in the run-up to elections. State discoms are the buyers of smart meters, distribution transformers and cables, funded largely by the central government's distribution reform scheme, which releases money only when discoms hit reform targets. That conditionality is why meter orders arrive in lumps.

Private demand is growing around the edges. Factories, housing projects and data centres buy cables, switchgear and private substations. Railways and metros buy traction lines and substations. And then there is the export tile, which has become one of the most interesting. The world, from America to Europe to the Gulf, is short of large transformers, as grids are rebuilt for renewables and data centres. Indian equipment makers have found themselves with export orders and pricing power they did not have a few years ago.

Finally the traders and exchanges, which buy short-term power and transmission corridor capacity during heatwaves and outages. That is PTC's world, and it is the one tile that moves with the weather rather than the budget.
c3.read:
Eight tiles, one per customer group. Each reads in three lines: who buys, what they buy, and what moves them.

The quickest way to use the grid is to sort the tiles by who decides the spending.

  • Plan-driven: the central planner and Power Grid, state transmission utilities, state discoms, railways and metros. Look at the third lines: the national transmission plan, state budgets, the distribution reform scheme, railway capex. These are policy calendars.
  • Private and global: renewable developers, industrial and real-estate customers, exports. Their third lines name renewable auctions, factory capex and housing, and the global transformer shortage.
  • Weather-driven: power exchanges and traders, moving with heatwaves, hydro and coal stock.

The first group is the bulk of demand, which is why the so-what under the grid says the budget speech, the national transmission plan and the renewable auction calendar matter more than any consumer number.

Then cross-reference with the doors in card one. Wire owners sell to essentially one tile, the central planner, through auctions and regulated projects. Cable and meter makers spread across discoms, private customers and exports. Traders live on the weather tile. A meter maker whose orders come almost entirely from the discom tile is a bet on the distribution reform scheme and on state utilities paying; one with a growing export tile has a second engine.

Keep the export tile in mind for card six, where the global transformer shortage appears as a dial of its own.

c4.story:
A transmission owner is a landlord whose rent is fixed by a government tribunal as a percentage of what the building cost. The tenant can never leave. The landlord's only real question is how many new buildings it can afford to put up, and at what interest rate.

That is why the owner's profit and loss statement looks so odd. Raw materials barely register; it is not buying anything to resell. People and maintenance are modest. The big line is depreciation and interest, the cost of the steel and the loan. But here is the twist: depreciation is itself built into the regulated tariff. The regulator lets the owner recover it, so it is not money lost but money recouped. Interest matters more. Owners run with roughly two-thirds of their assets funded by debt, so every point of borrowing cost is a point of return. And the InvIT, which pays out most of its cash, trades against the government bond: when yields fall, its price rises.

For a wire owner, profit grows only when a line is switched on. Everything before that is just money in the ground.

The number that moves an owner's stock is capitalisation, the moment a finished line is energised and moves from capital work in progress into the regulated asset base, where it starts earning. Capex tells you what is being spent; capitalisation tells you what has started to pay.

The cable maker is the hardware shop next door. Metal is the overwhelming majority of its sales, and its whole margin lives in the gap between the copper or aluminium price on the day it quoted and the day it delivered. A tender won just before aluminium jumped is a loss delivered months later. Contractors and meter makers add one more risk: working capital. They wait on state utilities to pay, and receivables stretching past a quarter are the first sign of trouble.
c4.read:
Two bar charts walk a hundred rupees of sales down to what is left: one for regulated wire owners, one for cable, conductor and meter makers. Read each left to right.

  • The input bar is raw materials and bought-in works. For the wire owner it is a tiny sliver. For the cable maker it is the giant bar, about seven of every ten rupees.
  • The opex bar is people, maintenance and freight: around a tenth for the owner, a bit more for the maker.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is where the owner's money goes: nearly a third of sales. For the maker it is a thin slice.
  • The last bar is what is left. For the owner, more than half of every rupee of sales. For the maker, about an eighth.

Put the two side by side and you are looking at the two extremes of business models: one almost all capital and no inputs, the other almost all inputs and little capital. That is why the so-what warns never to judge one door by the other's numbers. These are illustrative mid-cycle shapes; hover a bar for the amount.

Below, the list marks which lines matter. Depreciation, interest, capex and working capital get a yes. Read the depreciation reason closely: for an owner it is recovered through the tariff, not lost. Raw materials get a sometimes, because they are everything for a cable maker and nothing for an owner. The availability incentive gets a sometimes too: a small bonus above a high availability threshold. Other income and tax get a no.

The checklist is in the so-what: for owners, read capitalisation and borrowing cost; for makers, read order book and gross margin.

c5.story:
The wire owners are barely cyclical. Everyone around them is, and the cycle they ride is not power demand. It is how much grid the government decides to build, and whether discoms can pay for it.

The last full lap began with a boom from 2007 to 2011. Private power plants were going up everywhere, Power Grid listed in 2007, the first private transmission bids were won, and tower and conductor makers sold out. It peaked in 2011 and 2012, when generation had been ordered far ahead of coal and buyers. Then came the bust: stranded power plants, bankrupt discoms, and competitive bids at punishing tariffs. EPC margins vanished. The bottom, from 2017 to 2020, was a time of discom bailouts and thin ordering, with Power Grid growing only through regulated projects.

The turn came in stages. In 2020, after Galwan, India curbed power equipment imports from neighbours that share a land border, shutting China out. In 2021 and 2022 the distribution reform scheme launched with prepaid smart meters at its heart, the late-payment rules forced discoms to pay or lose supply, Power Grid spun its operating lines into an InvIT, and the planner published the roadmap to connect half a terawatt of renewables.

Then the boom arrived, in 2023 and 2024. Transmission tenders worth several years of history were bid in a single year. Power Grid tripled its capex guidance. Smart-meter awards ran into crores of units. A global transformer shortage lifted every equipment maker, and cable and conductor stocks re-rated hard.

By 2025 the boom hit a wall, not of money but of things. Transformer steel was short, right of way slow, and smart-meter rollouts stalled in some states as consumers pushed back on prepaid meters. Rate cuts lowered owners' borrowing costs. In 2026, order books remain at records. The constraint is execution.
c5.read:
Three pieces: the clock, the timeline and the four hands.

The clock has four arcs, clockwise from the top: boom, peak, bust and bottom. The years under each come from the previous lap: boom from 2007 to 2011, peak in 2011 and 2012, bust from 2013 to 2016, bottom from 2017 to 2020. The arrow points into the middle of the boom arc, on the upper right, labelled capex boom, supply-tight, with the detail record orders, execution and metal constrained. Compare that with oil, gas and power generation, whose arrows sit at a peak or a bottom: this is the energy industry squarely inside its boom.

The timeline runs from 2019. Read the colours: bust in 2019, then three neutral entries, 2020 and 2021 to 2022, which were the quiet set-up years of import curbs, reform schemes and the InvIT. Then boom for 2023 and 2024, neutral for 2025 as execution hit the wall, and now for 2026. Notice that the boom was built on rules passed in the neutral years; the policy came first, the orders followed.

The four hands tell you how long the boom lasts.

  • Transmission tenders awarded: record but slowing, pointing up. A fall would mean the plan has largely been bid out.
  • Power Grid capitalisation against capex: capex running ahead, a mixed reading. When capitalisation catches up, earnings follow.
  • Aluminium and transformer-steel prices: firm, pointing down for makers on fixed-price orders.
  • Discom receivable days: improving, pointing up.

The so-what reads the hands for you: in a supply-tight boom, money goes first to whoever has spare capacity in transformers, conductors and meters, and only later to owners whose assets take years to energise.

c6.story:
Three forces decide this industry's fortunes, and only one of them has anything to do with electricity.

The first is the price of money. For wire owners, borrowing cost is the spread: they earn a regulated return on equity and pay interest on the debt that funds most of the asset. Cheaper money widens the gap. For the InvIT, which investors treat like a bond, falling yields mean a higher price. That is why the bond yield is a three-dot dial: it moves the biggest names in the industry more than any power statistic.

The second is renewable capacity additions. Every solar park needs a line to carry its power out, so renewable auctions pull transmission orders forward. The third is government capex: the budget funds Power Grid's plans, the distribution reform scheme and state utilities. When the government spends, order books fill across all three doors.

Then the metal dials. Aluminium is the main metal in conductors, copper goes into cables, windings and meters, and both carry a diamond: a rise squeezes makers on fixed-price orders, but it also lifts the value of new orders and the inventory makers already hold. Power demand growth strengthens the case for more grid. Discom finances decide whether the payer of last resort pays. And the global transformer shortage gives Indian makers export orders and pricing power.

The one-dot dials are the rupee, which raises the cost of imported transformer steel and HVDC gear, and the revival of coal plants, which adds a second leg of transmission demand, because new thermal plants need evacuation too.
c6.read:
Each row is a dial. Read across: the dial, its channel, what a rise does, and its weight in dots.

  • The arrows: green up means a rise helps, red down means it hurts, a diamond means mixed. Aluminium and copper carry diamonds. Interest rates and the rupee are the red rows.
  • The weights: three dots for interest rates, renewable additions and government capex.

Look at the three three-dot rows together. One is the price of money, two are the order book. That is a neat summary of the whole industry: owners care about the first, makers and contractors about the other two.

Today's reading column is better populated here than in most industries. Interest rates map to the money-market rate, aluminium and copper to their own prices, power demand to the electricity component of industrial output, the rupee to the dollar rate, and the coal revival to the core-sector coal index. Two are proxies: renewable capacity additions map to the core-sector electricity index, and government capex maps to the Nifty Infrastructure index, which is the market's view of the infra trade rather than spending itself. Discom finances and the global transformer shortage show a dash; follow those through company commentary and news.

The so-what tells you how to boil the table down: track the bond yield for the owners, and transmission tender awards for everyone else. One is the price of money, the other is the order book. Tender awards are not a row here because they are an event, not a macro series; you will find them on card eleven's lead-time chart, sitting far to the right.

c7.story:
India's grid boom has plenty of money behind it. What it lacks is land, steel and time.

Start with right of way, the legal permission to run a line across land you do not own. Farmers want compensation. Forests need clearances. Cities have no room. And sometimes a bird gets a vote. In 2021 the Supreme Court, hearing a case on the critically endangered great Indian bustard, which collides with power lines in the Rajasthan and Gujarat deserts, ordered lines in its habitat to be put underground where feasible, right in the middle of India's best solar country. The order was later eased, but the episode showed how a single court case can stall a corridor. Disputes like these routinely add a year or two to a project.

In transmission, the expensive part is not the tower. It is the permission to stand it somewhere.

Then steel and transformers. India imports most of the special CRGO steel that goes into transformer cores, and the whole world is short of large transformers. During the boom, delivery times stretched from months to years. That is a cyclical bottleneck: it will ease when supply catches up, and when it does, equipment makers' pricing power will ease with it. Stringing crews and tower fabricators are finite too, and a boom bids both up.

The structural risks are two. Discom payment discipline: discoms lose money on every unit sold to farms and homes, and while the late-payment rules have helped, a state election can undo a year of discipline. And concentration: two companies own most of the inter-state grid, one a government company, the other part of the Adani group, whose headlines, from the Hindenburg report in 2023 to the US indictment in 2024, have moved its stock far more than its wires have.

Finally, competitive bidding cuts both ways, and smart meters are proving slow: states must install them, consumers accept them, and discoms pay for them.
c7.read:
Each row is a bottleneck, why it bites, and a severity tag. The tag tells you how to hold the risk.

  • Structural: right of way, discom payment discipline, and concentration and group risk. Three structural rows, more than in most industries. The first sets the pace of every project, the second the credit quality of every receivable, the third the headline risk in the industry's second-largest name.
  • Cyclical: transformer steel and EPC labour. These are the boom's own bottlenecks. They are why makers with spare capacity are winning now, and they are also the reason that pricing power will fade when supply catches up.
  • Two-sided: competitive bidding. When money is cheap, bids are aggressive and lock in thin returns for decades; when money is dear, bids become sensible. Good for owners in one rate regime, bad in another.
  • Slow: the smart-meter rollout. Real orders, slow conversion to revenue.

Now map rows to doors. Owners care about right of way, which delays capitalisation, and about bidding discipline. Makers care about steel, labour and the transformer queue. Meter makers and contractors care about discom payments and the smart-meter pace. Everyone is exposed to the concentration row indirectly, because a shock to one big owner affects orders across the chain.

The so-what puts it in one line: right of way and discom finances set the pace for good; the transformer shortage and bidding wars decide who makes money in this particular boom.

c8.story:
In transmission, the business model is written in a regulation. Literally.

The central regulator, CERC, issues a tariff order every five years that sets the rules for inter-state lines: the allowed return on equity, the availability threshold above which an owner earns a bonus, and the penalty below it. That document is the owners' profit formula. State regulators do the same for intra-state lines and, more importantly, set the tariffs that decide whether a discom can afford to pay its suppliers.

Most new inter-state lines, though, are not handed to Power Grid on a cost-plus basis. They are auctioned under tariff-based competitive bidding, run by the consulting arms of PFC and REC: whoever offers the lowest annual tariff for thirty-five years wins. The return a new line earns is decided on auction day, for its whole life.

The boom itself was created by a handful of rules. The General Network Access rules let a generator book grid capacity without first having a buyer, so lines can be planned ahead of plants. That is why orders are so big. The Ministry of Power and the Central Electricity Authority publish the national transmission plan, which is in effect the order pipeline for the next decade. The late-payment rules turned the sector's worst receivable, the discom, into something close to a sovereign one. And the Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme, launched in 2021, pays for prepaid smart meters and loss reduction, but only against reform milestones, so the meter order book hangs on it.

The import curbs on equipment from neighbouring countries, in place since 2020, protect Indian makers and lengthen the transformer queue. And one big rule is still coming: the Electricity Amendment Bill, introduced in 2022, which would let competing licensees distribute power in the same area. That could create private buyers for cables and meters, and private payers, which would be a change of character for the whole chain.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or a rule: what it does, why you care, and its status.

  • Always: CERC, the state regulators and competitive bidding. The permanent architecture. CERC's five-year order sets the owners' return; the bidding regime sets the return on each new line.
  • Live: the Ministry of Power and CEA plan, the late-payment rules, the distribution reform scheme, General Network Access and the import curbs. Five live rows, and almost all of them are why the boom exists. This is an industry whose order book was legislated into being.
  • Coming: the Electricity Amendment Bill. Slow and uncertain, but the one row that could change who pays at the end of the chain.

Sort the rows by door to see the exposure. Owners live under CERC, competitive bidding and the late-payment rules. Makers live under the transmission plan, the distribution reform scheme and the import curbs. Meter makers in particular hang almost entirely on the reform scheme row. Contractors live under the plan and under discom payments.

Read the why-you-care column for the late-payment rules carefully: it says they turned the worst receivable into a near-sovereign one. If that rule ever weakened, three of the doors would feel it at once, which is why a state election cycle unwinding discom discipline is one of the would-change items in the call.

Dated regulatory news filtered for this industry sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Run a transmission owner through Porter's five forces and you get one of the calmest shapes on this whole page, with one interesting bulge.

Rivalry is low because owners fight only at the auction. Once a line is won, it is a monopoly for decades: nobody builds a second line next to yours to compete on price. Buyer power is weak because owners are paid through a pooled, rule-protected mechanism: inter-state transmission charges are collected from all users together and passed to owners, and the late-payment rules back it up. Substitutes barely exist. Batteries and local generation can delay a line; they cannot replace one. Nothing replaces a wire.

So where is the bulge? New entrants. When money is cheap, pension funds, sovereign funds and infrastructure trusts love a thirty-five-year regulated cash flow, and they bid for new lines aggressively. That pushes down the tariffs on new projects and squeezes the returns owners can earn on growth. The existing lines are safe; the next ones are contested.

A transmission line is a monopoly after the auction and a knife fight before it.

The makers and contractors live in a much harsher world. They fight on every tender, so rivalry is high. Their suppliers are a few metal producers and imported transformer steel, so supplier power is high. Their buyers, Power Grid and state utilities, dictate terms, so buyer power is high too. New conductor and meter capacity takes a year or two to build, and China is kept out by policy, which helps, but only for as long as the policy lasts.

The so-what lands the point: owners keep the profit because the regulator guarantees it, makers keep it only while supply is short, and contractors rarely keep it at all.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes: rivalry at the top, then clockwise supplier power, buyer power, new entrants and substitutes. The further a shape reaches out, the more pressure that force applies. Smaller shape, better business.

Two shapes: regulated wire owners, and cables, conductors, meters and EPC combined. The makers' shape is the big one, reaching two and a half on rivalry, supplier power and buyer power, the three spokes across the top and right. That is the shape of a business squeezed from every commercial side.

The owners' shape is much smaller: one and a half on rivalry and supplier power, a single point on buyer power, and just half a point on substitutes, almost the centre. Now look at the lower-left spoke, new entrants. Both shapes reach exactly two. That is the one place where the two shapes touch, and it is the bulge from the story: cheap money brings new bidders for lines, just as new capacity eventually arrives for makers.

So read the chart as two stories. On the commercial spokes, owners are protected and makers are exposed. On the entrants spoke, both face the same pressure, from different directions.

The table beside the chart gives each score with a one-line reason. Adjust for a specific company: an owner with mostly regulated, cost-plus assets, rather than competitively bid ones, would pull in its entrants spoke; a maker with export orders and spare capacity during the transformer shortage would pull in its buyer spoke, at least until supply catches up.

c10.story:
Power Grid's results day has one number that matters more than the rest, and it is not profit. It is capitalisation: how much new asset was switched on in the quarter and moved into the regulated base, where it starts earning. Capex tells you what was spent. Capitalisation tells you what started to pay. When capex runs far ahead of capitalisation for a long time, projects are delayed, and earnings growth will lag the headline spending. Read capex to depreciation alongside it to see whether an owner is building hard or coasting.

Next, line availability. Owners earn an incentive above a high availability threshold, so availability near the top of the range is quiet money, and a dip below the threshold is a penalty. Then the EBITDA margin, which in this industry mostly tells you which door a company is really behind: owners run margins far above makers, and makers above contractors. A company claiming to be an owner with a maker's margin deserves a second look at its segment table.

Debt is not a warning sign for an owner; it is the business model. Net debt to EBITDA tells you how much room an owner has to bid for new lines, and for a maker how much financial cushion it has. Receivable days tell you whether state utilities are paying, and for meter makers and contractors they are the first number to check.

For makers and contractors, two more. Order book to sales gives visibility: a couple of years of work is comfortable, much more means execution risk, much less means a cliff. And gross margin on cables and conductors tells you whether metal moved against orders already booked. A margin falling while aluminium rose is fixed-price pain arriving on schedule.
c10.read:
One row per number: what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median from listed companies' latest annual filings.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask. Notice the split: capitalisation, availability and debt rows are mostly about owners; order book and cable gross margin are about makers; receivables touch everyone.
  • What good looks like gives the rules of thumb: capex above twice depreciation for owners in this boom, availability above the high nineties, EBITDA margins above four-fifths for owners and around a tenth for makers and contractors, owner debt under four times EBITDA, receivables under two months for owners and four for meter makers and EPC, and an order book of two to three years of sales. Benchmarks, not targets.
  • Today's industry median fills where the number maps to a filing line.

Two rows show a dash: line availability and order book to sales, which come from company disclosures rather than financial statements. The capitalisation row shows a median of capital work in progress against gross block, a proxy: a high reading means a lot of asset is under construction and not yet earning, which is exactly the capex-ahead-of-capitalisation gap the clock's hand describes.

Remember that the medians blend owners, makers and traders. The median EBITDA margin falls somewhere between Power Grid and a cable maker and describes neither. Compare a company first with the good mark for its own door; use the median mainly for the receivables row, which tells you whether discom discipline is holding across the industry.

c11.story:
If oil is the industry where warnings arrive at the last minute, transmission is the opposite. Here the early signals are loud, public and three quarters ahead.

A transmission tender notice from the PFC and REC consulting arms becomes an award, and the award becomes orders for towers, conductors and transformers, a process that takes the better part of a year. Renewable auction results and solar park land allotments are transmission orders in disguise: a park awarded today needs its evacuation line ordered within a year. And every revision to the national transmission plan is tomorrow's tender list. All three sit at the far right of the chart.

Smart-meter tender awards by state speak two quarters ahead, because an award becomes meter revenue over the following couple of years. Then the one-quarter signals: aluminium and copper prices, because metal bought today is delivered against orders priced earlier; discom dues on the government's payment portal, falling dues meaning cash for meters and works; global transformer lead times, which signal export demand and pricing power; and the RBI policy rate, which lowers owners' interest cost and lifts the InvIT within a quarter.

Now the rule. The industry is in an up-cycle when transmission awards keep rising, capitalisation is catching up with capex, and discom dues are falling. Two of the three are on: awards are at a record pace, though plateauing, and dues are falling as the late-payment rules hold. The missing sign is capitalisation: capex is still running ahead. Two of three means the boom is maturing.

Hence the call: prefer the regulated owners and the equipment makers with spare capacity over fixed-price contractors, and treat the InvIT as a bond proxy that benefits from rate cuts. The constraint has moved from money to transformers, steel and right of way, and whoever already has capacity wins.

The chart places each outside signal by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot sits, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot for the channel it travels through.

Look at the shape first. Three dots sit at the far right, three quarters or more ahead: tender notices, renewable auction results and transmission plan revisions. That is unusual. In most industries the right-hand side of this chart is sparse; here it is where the action is. It means you can see this industry's order flow coming earlier than almost any other on the page.

One dot, smart-meter awards, sits at two quarters. The rest, metal prices, discom dues, transformer lead times and the policy rate, sit at one quarter. Use the chart as a reading order: the right-hand dots tell you about orders next year, the left-hand dots about margins and cash next quarter.

Below the chart, the rule shows three signs. Transmission awards rising has a tick: record pace, plateauing. Capitalisation catching capex has a cross: capex running ahead. Discom dues falling has a tick: late-payment rules holding. Two ticks match the rule's reading of a maturing boom, and the word plateauing on the first tick is worth watching, because if it turns into a cross, the rule drops to one of three, a boom ending.

The call box gives the headline, three points and the would-change list: a sharp rise in bond yields, a state election cycle unwinding discom discipline, and transformer and steel supply normalising. Set those as alerts. The first would hit owners, the second contractors and meter makers, the third the equipment makers' pricing power.
